what: Motor A moves a guided sled beneath a separate rubber measuring wheel. The wheel turns freely: contact with the passing surface supplies its rotation. Follow both the sled and one of the wheel’s visible spokes, then compare with the supplied model that holds the wheel clear of the surface.
try: Load travel-dial.ldr and its matching travel-dial.bw program. Reset the saved model, then press Run in Robot Lab’s toolbar. Follow the sled’s outward stroke and return.

Compare the six programmed arrivals: +60°, −60°, 0° at 15°/s, then the same route at 45°/s. The slider-crank makes sled speed vary along each stroke. For the same actual surface travel, should the measuring wheel need the same angle or the same time?
Predict the lifted-wheel result before loading the physical comparison model. Use the same program and compare actual sled travel as well as wheel motion.
Reset before repeating after an interruption or manual movement. Keep the supplied stroke limits; watch the independent wheel instead of treating the drive motor’s encoder as its reading.
why: Without slip, relative surface travel equals the rolling radius multiplied by the wheel’s angle in radians. Friction makes that relationship possible, but does not guarantee perfect tracking. A freely pivoting support can shift the wheel centre slightly, so the relevant travel is the surface’s motion relative to that centre. Lifting the wheel interrupts the intended contact path.
matters: Measuring wheels convert linear travel into a rotation that can be read by a pointer or encoder. Contact, alignment, effective radius and slip determine the usefulness of that measurement. A drive motor reaching its target does not establish what the separate measuring wheel recorded.
question: If the sled covers the same distance twice as quickly, should an ideal wheel rotate through twice the angle? What should happen when the wheel is held clear?
answer: The ideal angle depends on relative distance, not duration: the wheel rotates through the same angle in less time. Its angular speed increases. With the wheel clear, that surface motion no longer drives the wheel. Real contact can slip or creep, so compare the actual traces rather than assuming either perfect rolling or exactly zero residual motion. In the supplied native run, the main’s largest rolling residual was 0.116 mm. The raised wheel rotated at most 0.116°, while matched sled endpoints differed by at most 0.0039 mm. These are observations of this finite native experiment; physical tyre calibration remains separate.
further: Compare measured wheel angle with independently observed surface travel throughout each stroke, including acceleration, reversal and return. Do not choose a fitted radius merely to make the curves agree.
A wheel that returns near its starting angle can still have had errors along the way. Check both the travel trace and the return.
Compare Cusp Lab’s rack-constrained rolling and Integral’s wheel on a rotating disk. Here a separate passive wheel measures a linear surface.
The native contact model does not calibrate a physical LEGO measuring instrument. Tyre deformation, wear, alignment and axle friction need separate hardware measurements.
formula: Ideal no-slip relation: Δs_relative = R Δθ, with θ in radians and positive wheel angle chosen in the positive surface-travel direction. Δs_relative = Δx_sled − Δx_wheel centre. Here R = 28 mm; residual = observed relative travel − R × observed absolute wheel angle relative to the chassis. The crank angle is not the measuring wheel’s angle.
